authority: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) / Cantonal Migration Office (Migrationsamt)
deadline_label: Before issuing a job offer to a non-EU/EFTA national
non_obvious_official_guidance: Switzerland distinguishes EU/EFTA nationals (covered by the Agreement on Free Movement of Persons, AFMP) from third-country nationals (subject to Swiss immigration law and annual cantonal quotas). EU/EFTA nationals have a registration right and do not require prior employer sponsorship; non-EU/EFTA nationals require a cantonal work permit approved by the cantonal migration office and forwarded to SEM for federal authorisation before entry.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Three critical traps: (1) Contract duration governs permit type for EU/EFTA nationals — a contract of exactly 364 days triggers an L short-duration permit; 365 days or more triggers a B permit with different registration obligations and Quellensteuer withholding tariff categories. (2) Non-EU permit approvals are subject to strictly enforced annual cantonal quotas (contingents) — some cantons exhaust their non-EU B permit quota early in the calendar year; issuing a job offer without confirming quota availability leaves HR unable to bring the employee in on time. (3) British nationals post-Brexit lost AFMP rights and are now treated as third-country nationals subject to the same quota and labour-market-test system as other non-EU nationals — a change many UK-based HR teams have not fully internalised.
non_obvious_action_required: Before issuing any offer to a non-EU/EFTA national, contact the target cantonal migration office to confirm B permit quota availability for the current year. For EU/EFTA nationals, classify contract duration on day one — this determines whether to register for an L or B permit and which Quellensteuer tariff category applies. UK nationals must be processed as non-EU nationals from the outset; do not use the AFMP pathway for UK employees.
source: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) – Work permits overview

authority: Cantonal Migration Office (Migrationsamt) → State Secretariat for Migration (SEM)
form_name: Cantonal employer application + SEM ZEMIS portal
deadline_label: At least 10–16 weeks before planned start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: The employer applies to the cantonal migration office on behalf of the non-EU/EFTA national. The canton verifies local labour market priority — Swiss and EU/EFTA candidates must be demonstrably unavailable for the role — then forwards the approved application to SEM for federal authorisation. Only after SEM approval can the employee apply for a national long-stay visa at the Swiss embassy or consulate in their country of residence.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The labour market priority test (Inländervorrang) is a substantive hurdle, not an administrative formality — the employer must document genuine recruitment efforts showing no qualified Swiss or EU/EFTA candidate was available. SECO inspections of compliance documentation have intensified since 2023. Employers who file without adequate records (date-stamped job postings, interview notes, written rejection justifications) face outright refusal or multi-month delays. The cantonal → SEM → visa sequence typically takes 10–16 weeks; committing to a start date before SEM authorisation is confirmed routinely results in breach-of-offer situations that expose the employer to legal liability.
non_obvious_action_required: Before filing, compile a complete recruitment dossier: date-stamped job advertisements on Swiss and EU portals (RAV/ORP, EURES), candidate review notes, and written justification for why the selected non-EU national's profile was not replicable locally. Do not commit to a start date until the SEM authorisation letter is received. For specialised or senior roles where the priority test may be contested, commission a Swiss immigration lawyer before filing.
source: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) – Third-country nationals: admission for gainful employment

authority: Einwohnerkontrolle / Office de la population (Gemeinde / commune)
deadline_label: Within 14 days of taking up residence
non_obvious_official_guidance: All persons taking up residence in Switzerland must register at the Einwohnerkontrolle (residents' registration office) of their Gemeinde (municipality / commune) within 14 days of arrival. Foreign nationals receive their cantonal residence permit sticker or card at or following this appointment. The registration address determines the employee's cantonal and communal tax domicile for the entire tax year.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The choice of Gemeinde at registration has significant and permanent financial consequences: cantonal and communal income and wealth tax rates vary enormously — the combined top marginal rate in Zug (Gemeinde Baar) is roughly half that in Geneva. An employee who registers in Geneva intending to move to Zug later is taxed at Geneva rates for the entire first year, even if they relocate after two weeks. The Anmeldung address also determines which Krankenkasse regional premium band applies — health insurance premiums differ by up to 30% between regions within the same canton. Both effects are locked in from day one and cannot be unwound retroactively.
non_obvious_action_required: If the employee has any flexibility on canton of residence, run a comparative cantonal income tax and health insurance premium calculation before the Anmeldung appointment — not after. Bring to the Anmeldung: passport or national ID, work contract, accommodation confirmation (lease or property deed), and for non-EU nationals the SEM authorisation letter. The cantonal permit sticker is issued at or shortly after the Anmeldung and must be in the passport before any international travel.
source: ch.ch – Registering with the municipal authorities

authority: Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) / Cantonal authority
form_name: Policy application direct to chosen Swiss insurer
deadline_label: Within 3 months of establishing residence — policy backdated to arrival date
non_obvious_official_guidance: All persons resident in Switzerland must take out basic mandatory health insurance (Grundversicherung / assurance de base) with a recognised Swiss insurer under the KVG/LAMal within 3 months of establishing residence. The policy is backdated to the date of arrival or Anmeldung, so premiums are owed from day one regardless of when the policy is taken out.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Three major non-obvious realities: (1) Swiss mandatory health insurance is paid by the employee as an individual monthly invoice to the insurer — unlike most European countries it is NOT collected via payroll or by the employer. Many relocated employees expect a payroll deduction and discover an overdue invoice only when the first premium notice arrives. (2) Employers may pay a subsidy but are not legally required to, and any employer subsidy is taxable income to the employee. (3) Dental treatment is explicitly excluded from the basic mandatory coverage and from most supplementary insurance for pre-existing conditions — employees from NHS or statutory dental-coverage countries are consistently unprepared for Swiss out-of-pocket dental costs, which are among the highest in Europe.
non_obvious_action_required: Brief every inbound employee on day one: health insurance is their individual monthly invoice, not a payroll deduction. Use the FOPH comparison tool (priminfo.ch) immediately after the Anmeldung — the commune address entered determines the regional premium band. Choose the insurer within the first week of arrival; the cantonal authority will administratively assign a default insurer (rarely best value) to anyone who misses the 3-month deadline, and premiums are still owed from day one.
source: Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) – Mandatory health insurance

step: EU/EFTA Permit B or L – Cantonal Registration
authority: Cantonal Migration Office (Migrationsamt / Service de la population)
form_name: EU/EFTA declaration of gainful employment (Meldung Erwerbstätigkeit EG/EFTA)
field_label: Permit B or L Document Number
deadline_label: Within 14 days of taking up residence (simultaneous with Anmeldung)
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU/EFTA nationals taking up gainful employment in Switzerland for more than 90 days must obtain a permit B (1-year renewable, for contracts of 365 days or more) or permit L (short-duration, for contracts up to 364 days) from the cantonal migration office. This is a registration right under the AFMP — no prior employer authorisation or quota approval is required.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Two common HR errors: (1) L-permit holders on consecutive contracts with the same employer may not remain on L permits indefinitely — after 12 cumulative months of Swiss employment, the cantonal migration office is entitled to reclassify the permit to a B regardless of contract duration, changing the Quellensteuer tariff category and opening new residency rights that the employee may not have anticipated. (2) The L permit expires on the contract end date, not after 364 days — a contract extension triggers an immediate permit classification review. HR must notify the cantonal migration office of any contract extension on the day the extension is signed, not at the next permit renewal date.
non_obvious_action_required: At any contract extension, immediately assess whether the cumulative Swiss employment period crosses the 12-month threshold and initiate a B permit reclassification if applicable. Instruct the employee to carry their cantonal permit document alongside their national ID or passport at all times — Swiss border control routinely checks permits at land crossings even for EU nationals arriving from Schengen countries.
source: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) – EU/EFTA nationals: rights of residence

authority: Cantonal AHV Compensation Fund (kantonale Ausgleichskasse / caisse cantonale de compensation)
form_name: Employee registration form (Anmeldung Arbeitnehmer); AHV number via Central Compensation Office (ZAS/CCAS)
non_obvious_official_guidance: All employers in Switzerland must be affiliated with a cantonal AHV compensation fund and must register each employee and deduct AHV/IV/EO contributions from salary. Employees are assigned a permanent 13-digit AHV insurance number by the Central Compensation Office (ZAS/CCAS). The combined AHV/IV/EO rate is 10.6% of gross salary split equally between employer and employee (5.3% each), plus unemployment insurance (ALV) at 2.2% total and mandatory accident insurance via SUVA or a private insurer.
non_obvious_actual_reality: A critical long-term consequence that is almost never explained to newly relocated employees: AHV contribution gaps — years without Swiss or treaty-country contributions — permanently reduce the Swiss old-age pension on a pro-rata basis. An employee arriving at age 40 has a 20-year gap that reduces their maximum Swiss AHV pension by approximately half, and this cannot be retroactively filled from abroad without specific treaty provisions. Swiss AHV does not offer voluntary catch-up contributions for employed persons. Additionally, if an employee has previously worked in Switzerland, their 13-digit AHV number is permanent — creating a duplicate number for a returning employee produces records that take months to untangle with the ZAS.
non_obvious_action_required: Before payroll setup, ask the employee whether they have previously worked in Switzerland; if yes, confirm the existing AHV number directly with the ZAS before creating any new record. Brief the employee on the pro-rata pension gap at onboarding. For inbound EU/EFTA employees, verify whether the applicable bilateral totalization treaty allows home-country contribution years to count toward Swiss AHV entitlement qualifying periods.

authority: Employer's Pension Foundation (Pensionskasse) / Federal Social Insurance Office (FSIO/BSV)
deadline_label: From first day of employment (mandatory above CHF 22,680 annual salary, 2024 threshold)
non_obvious_official_guidance: All employees aged 17–70 earning above the BVG entry threshold (CHF 22,680/year in 2024) must be enrolled in a Pensionskasse (occupational pension fund) under the Federal Law on Occupational Retirement, Survivors' and Disability Pension Plans (BVG/LPP). Employer contributions are mandatory and must at minimum match the employee's own contribution.
non_obvious_actual_reality: On leaving Switzerland, BVG capital is not simply repatriated — it is transferred to a Freizügigkeitskonto (vested benefits account) at a Swiss bank or insurance company, and direct payout to a foreign account is heavily restricted for employees under retirement age. For departures to EU/EFTA countries, treaty provisions may allow transfer but the process takes 3–6 months; employees who leave without initiating it find funds inaccessible for years. For departures to non-treaty countries (US, UK post-Brexit, Canada), a lump-sum payout triggers a flat 5% Swiss withholding tax on the mandatory BVG portion. Separately, the Pillar 3a voluntary contribution (up to CHF 7,056/year for employed persons in 2024) is fully deductible from cantonal and federal taxable income — an employee who delays account opening past 31 December of the first Swiss tax year loses that year's deduction permanently.
non_obvious_action_required: Enrol the employee in the Pensionskasse on day one and confirm the employer contribution rate — many Swiss employers contribute above the BVG minimum. Brief the employee on the Freizügigkeitskonto process at the start of employment, not on the last day. Recommend opening a Pillar 3a account at a Swiss bank or PostFinance before 31 December of the first tax year; account opening takes one to two business days.
source: Federal Social Insurance Office (FSIO/BSV) – Occupational pension BVG/LPP

step: Quellensteuer – Withholding Tax at Source Registration
authority: Cantonal Tax Authority (Steuerverwaltung / Administration fiscale cantonale)
form_name: Employer notification of withholding obligation; cantonal tariff classification declaration
deadline_label: Before first payroll run — employer must apply the correct cantonal tariff from day one
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreign nationals holding a permit B, L, or G who are not subject to ordinary assessment are liable to Quellensteuer (withholding tax at source). The employer deducts tax from salary using canton-specific tariff tables and remits it monthly to the cantonal tax authority. Permit C holders and Swiss nationals fall under the ordinary cantonal and federal assessment process instead.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Two major non-obvious traps: (1) Employees earning above CHF 120,000 gross per year are subject to mandatory subsequent ordinary assessment (nachträgliche ordentliche Veranlagung, NOV) even while nominally on Quellensteuer — the employer still withholds at source but the employee must file a full cantonal and federal tax return to reconcile. Many employees and HR teams assume Quellensteuer fully discharges the Swiss tax obligation and are surprised by the mandatory filing and potential year-end surcharge or refund. (2) Expatriate expense allowances under ESTV Circular 40 — housing cost differentials, international school fees for expat children, home-leave flights — can reduce the Quellensteuer tariff base only if a formal request is filed with the cantonal tax authority before payroll runs; they are never applied automatically even when the employer reports them on the salary certificate.
non_obvious_action_required: At onboarding, check whether the employee's anticipated gross annual salary exceeds CHF 120,000 — if so, notify them immediately that a full cantonal and federal tax return (NOV) will be required regardless of source withholding. If the employer provides expatriate allowances, file for ESTV Circular 40 expatriate deduction approval with the cantonal tax authority before the first payroll run. Confirm the correct tariff code with payroll (marital status, number of dependants, single- or dual-income household) — incorrect codes create year-end true-up liabilities that are difficult to reverse.
source: Federal Tax Administration (FTA) – Withholding tax for foreign nationals (Quellensteuer)

step: Annual Cantonal and Federal Tax Return (Ordinary Assessment / NOV)
authority: Cantonal Tax Authority (Steuerverwaltung) + Federal Tax Administration (ESTV)
form_name: Cantonal income and wealth tax return (canton-specific); direct federal tax declaration (DBSt/IFD)
deadline_label: 31 March of the following year (cantonal); extensions routinely granted on request
non_obvious_official_guidance: Permit C holders, Swiss nationals, and permit B holders earning above CHF 120,000/year (NOV threshold) must file an annual cantonal and federal income tax return. The canton issues a combined assessment covering cantonal, communal, and — acting as federal collection agent — direct federal tax (DBSt). Switzerland taxes worldwide income for all Swiss tax residents.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Three compounding non-obvious realities: (1) The three-tier tax system (federal + cantonal + communal) means effective combined marginal rates depend entirely on the specific Gemeinde of registration — the same CHF 250,000 income attracts approximately 22% combined in Zug (Baar) but 42% in Geneva; the difference on a senior package is larger than most HR teams realise. (2) Switzerland taxes worldwide income including foreign dividend income, overseas rental income, and gains on foreign investment accounts — many inbound employees from the UK, Germany, and France assume home-country assets are invisible to Swiss authorities; they are not, because Switzerland participates in OECD CRS/AEOI automatic exchange of financial account information. (3) The ESTV Circular 40 expatriate lump-sum deduction (housing cost differential above home-country norm, international school fees, home-leave costs) reduces taxable income but must be claimed proactively in the return — it is never applied automatically by the tax authority.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a Swiss tax adviser in the first Swiss tax year — not at filing time — to assess worldwide income exposure and identify all applicable deductions including ESTV Circular 40 allowances. Provide the adviser with full data on foreign investment accounts, rental properties, and pension fund values as at 31 December. Request a deadline extension from the cantonal authority by 31 March — most cantons grant 3–6 month extensions on first request without penalty.
source: Federal Tax Administration (FTA) – Direct federal tax (DBSt)

step: Wealth Tax (Vermögenssteuer / Impôt sur la fortune) – Annual Declaration
authority: Cantonal Tax Authority (Steuerverwaltung / Administration fiscale cantonale)
form_name: Wealth declaration section of the annual cantonal tax return
field_label: Net Taxable Wealth (Netto-Reinvermögen / Fortune nette imposable)
deadline_label: Declared in the annual cantonal tax return (31 March deadline, same as income tax)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Switzerland levies an annual cantonal and communal wealth tax (Vermögenssteuer / impôt sur la fortune) on the worldwide net assets of Swiss tax residents. Taxable assets include real estate, bank and investment accounts, securities, business interests, vehicles, and valuables, net of deductible liabilities. BVG Pillar 2 pension assets and Pillar 3a accounts are excluded in most cantons. The federal government does not levy a wealth tax — it is exclusively a cantonal and communal instrument, with rates and exemption thresholds set independently by each canton.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Switzerland is the only major European country with a universal annual wealth tax on all residents. Newly relocated employees from Germany, France, the UK, and the US have never encountered this concept and are routinely unaware of it until a tax inspection or adviser raises it. A typical inbound profile — a family home in the origin country, a UK or German pension pot, and a share portfolio — can easily generate a six-figure Swiss taxable wealth figure from day one of Swiss tax residence. In Zug the rate on that wealth may be negligible (below 0.15% above exemption). In Geneva the rate on net wealth above CHF 1 million reaches approximately 1% per year — a material annual liability. The declaration requires market-value assessments of all worldwide assets as at 31 December each year, including foreign pension funds, which some cantons assess at full capital value under specific bilateral treaty provisions.
non_obvious_action_required: Disclose the wealth tax obligation explicitly to every inbound employee at the first onboarding briefing — do not assume they know it exists. Ask the employee to prepare a preliminary list of worldwide assets (property market values, pension fund estimates, investment account balances as at 31 December) in the first Swiss tax year and provide this to a Swiss tax adviser before filing. Alert the employee that foreign pension funds may be partially or fully declarable depending on canton and applicable treaty — this must be assessed by a qualified Swiss tax adviser before the return is filed.
source: Federal Tax Administration (FTA) – Swiss tax system overview (cantonal taxes)

step: Permit B Renewal and C-Permit Eligibility Tracking
authority: Cantonal Migration Office (Migrationsamt / Service de la population)
field_label: Renewed Permit B Expiry Date / C-Permit Issue Date
deadline_label: File renewal at least 14 days before expiry; initiate process 3 months before
non_obvious_official_guidance: Permit B (annual residence permit for gainful employment) must be renewed before expiry. EU/EFTA nationals renew as of right provided they remain employed or are actively and demonstrably job-seeking. Non-EU nationals face a substantive cantonal review at each renewal. After 5 consecutive years of legal residence, non-EU nationals from most countries become eligible to apply for a settlement permit C.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Two major long-term flags that HR consistently misses: (1) Non-EU nationals face a substantive re-assessment of labour-market conditions and employer standing at each B permit renewal — changed economic circumstances or employer financial difficulties can result in refusal in a way that EU/EFTA renewals cannot. (2) The transition from permit B to permit C is a major financial event: it switches the employee from Quellensteuer withholding to ordinary cantonal and federal assessment, changes payroll obligations, and requires the employee to file a full tax return for the first time. HR teams routinely miss the 5-year eligibility date and fail to advise the employee or update payroll accordingly. The C-permit switch cannot be backdated — every year of delay is a year the employee may be incorrectly withheld under Quellensteuer.
non_obvious_action_required: Track every non-EU employee's 5-year continuous-residence date in the HR system alongside the permit expiry date. At the 5-year mark, notify the employee of C-permit eligibility and initiate the application — do not wait for the employee to raise it. On C-permit approval, immediately notify payroll to switch from Quellensteuer to ordinary assessment and inform the cantonal tax authority. Set HR calendar alerts at 3 months before every permit expiry — not the 14-day statutory minimum.
source: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) – Permit types and renewal

step: AHV Totalization & A1 Certificate – Posted Workers
authority: Swiss Compensation Office (SAK/ZAS) / Home-country social security authority
form_name: A1 Certificate (EU/EFTA postings) / Certificate of Coverage (bilateral treaty, non-EU)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Workers temporarily posted to Switzerland by a foreign EU/EFTA employer may remain in their home-country social security system — avoiding Swiss AHV contributions — if an A1 certificate is obtained before work begins in Switzerland, under Regulation (EC) 883/2004 as incorporated into the AFMP. Switzerland also has bilateral totalization agreements with numerous non-EU countries (US, Canada, Australia, India, Japan) providing equivalent exemptions via Certificates of Coverage.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Four non-obvious realities: (1) Switzerland is not an EU member but is fully bound by Regulation 883/2004 via the AFMP — HR teams with no prior Swiss experience frequently assume EU social security coordination rules do not apply in Switzerland; they do. (2) British nationals posted to Switzerland must now use the UK-Switzerland bilateral social security agreement (signed 2021) rather than the AFMP mechanism — a different form set, a different competent authority (HMRC for the UK side), and longer processing times. (3) A1 posting authorisations are limited to a maximum of 24 months; exceeding this limit without a bilateral extension agreement creates retroactive dual-contribution liability in both countries and Swiss penalty exposure from the date of the breach. (4) The A1 mechanism covers only social security exemption — it does not determine where income tax is paid, which is governed separately by the applicable double-taxation treaty (DTT); HR teams frequently conflate the two.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply for the A1 (EU/EFTA employees) or Certificate of Coverage (bilateral treaty employees) from the home-country social security authority before the employee's first Swiss working day — not after. For UK nationals, use the HMRC bilateral form set under the UK-CH agreement (not the standard EU A1 process). Calendar the 24-month posting duration limit and apply for any bilateral extension 3 months before expiry. For permanent transfers as opposed to postings, cease home-country social security contributions and register the employee with the Swiss cantonal AHV compensation fund from day one.
source: Swiss Compensation Office (SAK/ZAS) – International social security agreements
